h: Unknown warrior, famous scientists and a gallery in the roof
p: Just inside the west door, surrounded by poppies, lies the Tomb of the Unknown Warrior, an unidentified soldier brought back from the battlefields of the First World War and buried here in 1920. It's the only tomb in the Abbey that people don't walk on, and it stops most visitors in their tracks. A little further in, Sir Isaac Newton's monument and the graves of Charles Darwin and other scientists show how the Abbey honours more than just royalty.

High above the nave, the Queen's Diamond Jubilee Galleries sit in the triforium, a space that was closed to the public for centuries. It's reached by its own tower and lift, and the views down into the Abbey are breathtaking. Treasures on display there help tell the story of coronations, royal funerals and the Abbey's long history. Access usually needs an extra timed ticket, so arrange that when you book.

Don't skip the cloisters and the octagonal Chapter House, with its medieval tiled floor and wall paintings. It's a calmer part of the visit and gives you a sense of the Abbey as a working monastery long before it became such a famous church. Allow around two hours for a relaxed look.

For a completely different way to experience it, Evensong in the late afternoon is free to attend and lets you hear the choir in that soaring space. Right opposite, the Jewel Tower is a surviving piece of the medieval Palace of Westminster, and the Churchill War Rooms on King Charles Street are a short walk away. St James's Park is perfect for a breather afterwards.
